opening.text: When a teenager is out late, many parents leave the porch light on. It is a small thing. But it says, “You are expected. You are welcome here. Come home.”
The Savior’s love is like that light. It is always on. It does not depend on how well we did today. I would like to talk about the love of Jesus Christ.

mainMessage.text: The love of Jesus Christ is real, and it is personal. The Father sent His Son because He loves us. The Son gave His life because He loves us. He holds out His arms. He knows our pain from the inside. And nothing we do can make Him stop loving us. When we feel that love, we want to love others the way He does.

blocks.text: The Father gave His Son.

John wrote the most loved verse in the Bible. God so loved the world that He gave His Son. And in his letter, John said it again. God’s love was shown when He sent Jesus so that we could live through Him. The love came first. We did not earn it.
For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.

In this was manifested the love of God toward us, because that God sent his only begotten Son into the world, that we might live through him. Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.
Elder Neal A. Maxwell of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his talk “Lessons from Laman and Lemuel” from the October 1999 general conference.

The tree of life . . . is the love of God (see 1 Ne. 11:25). The love of God for His children is most profoundly expressed in His gift of Jesus as our Redeemer: ‘God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son’ (John 3:16). To partake of the love of God is to partake of Jesus’ Atonement and the emancipations and joys which it can bring.
The Atonement is the gift. Love is the reason.
He gave His own life.

Jesus called Himself the good shepherd. A good shepherd stays with the sheep, even when it costs him. Jesus said He knows His sheep, and that He would lay down His life for them. Then He said that no one has greater love than this.

I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep. . . . I am the good shepherd, and know my sheep, and am known of mine. As the Father knoweth me, even so know I the Father: and I lay down my life for the sheep.
Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
Elder David B. Haight of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles asked this in his article “Remembering the Savior’s Atonement” in the April 1988 Ensign. It is a magazine article, not a conference talk.
How are we doing as members of the Church in remembering our Lord and Savior, His sacrifice, and our indebtedness to Him?
It is a fair question. We remember because we are grateful.
His arms are open.

Two Book of Mormon writers used the same picture. Lehi said he was encircled in the arms of His love. Mormon said that some will wish they had been clasped in the arms of Jesus. The invitation is there. We only have to come.
But behold, the Lord hath redeemed my soul from hell; I have beheld his glory, and I am encircled about eternally in the arms of his love.

For I know that such will sorrow for the calamity of the house of Israel; yea, they will sorrow for the destruction of this people; they will sorrow that this people had not repented that they might have been clasped in the arms of Jesus.
Elder Russell M. Nelson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his talk “The Atonement” from the October 1996 general conference.

Rich meaning is found in study of the word atonement in the Semitic languages of Old Testament times. In Hebrew, the basic word for atonement is kaphar, a verb that means ‘to cover’ or ‘to forgive.’ Closely related is the Aramaic and Arabic word kafat, meaning ‘a close embrace’—no doubt related to the Egyptian ritual embrace. References to that embrace are evident in the Book of Mormon. One states that ‘the Lord hath redeemed my soul . . . ; I have beheld his glory, and I am encircled about eternally in the arms of his love.’ \[2 Nephi 1:15.\] Another proffers the glorious hope of our being ‘clasped in the arms of Jesus.’ \[Mormon 5:11.\]
Atonement means a close embrace. That is how near He wants to be.
He knows how it feels.

Some days we think no one understands. The Savior does. Alma taught that He took our pains, sicknesses, and weaknesses upon Him so that He would know how to help us. And through Isaiah, the Lord said He would never forget us. He has written us on the palms of His hands.

And he shall go forth, suffering pains and afflictions and temptations of every kind; and this that the word might be fulfilled which saith he will take upon him the pains and the sicknesses of his people. And he will take upon him death, that he may loose the bands of death which bind his people; and he will take upon him their infirmities, that his bowels may be filled with mercy, according to the flesh, that he may know according to the flesh how to succor his people according to their infirmities.

Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee. Behold, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands; thy walls are continually before me.
Elder Richard G. Scott of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his talk “To Be Healed” from the April 1994 general conference.

Faith in Christ means we trust Him; we trust His teachings. That leads to hope, and hope brings charity, the pure love of Christ—that peaceful feeling that comes when we sense His concern, His love, and His capacity to cure us or to ease our burdens with His healing power.
He is not far away. He is close, and He cares.
His love does not quit.

Paul listed everything he could think of: death, life, angels, powers, things now, things to come. None of it can separate us from the love of God in Christ. And Nephi quoted the Lord saying His arm is stretched out all the day long.

For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

Wo be unto the Gentiles, saith the Lord God of Hosts! For notwithstanding I shall lengthen out mine arm unto them from day to day, they will deny me; nevertheless, I will be merciful unto them, saith the Lord God, if they will repent and come unto me; for mine arm is lengthened out all the day long, saith the Lord God of Hosts.
Elder Jeffrey R. Holland of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his talk “Prophets in the Land Again” from the October 2006 general conference.

To all of you who think you are lost or without hope, or who think you have done too much that was too wrong for too long, to every one of you who worry that you are stranded somewhere on the wintry plains of life and have wrecked your handcart in the process, this conference calls out Jehovah’s unrelenting refrain, ‘\[My\] hand is stretched out still’ \[see Isaiah 5:25; 9:17, 21\]. ‘I shall lengthen out mine arm unto them,’ He said, ‘\[and even if they\] deny me; nevertheless, I will be merciful unto them, . . . if they will repent and come unto me; for mine arm is lengthened out all the day long, saith the Lord God of Hosts’ \[2 Nephi 28:32\]. His mercy endureth forever, and His hand is stretched out still. His is the pure love of Christ, the charity that never faileth, that compassion which endures even when all other strength disappears \[see Moroni 7:46–47\].
His hand is stretched out still. That is good news.
We love because He loved us.
Jesus gave His disciples a new commandment. Love one another as I have loved you. John said it simply: we love Him because He first loved us. The love flows down, and then it flows out.
A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another. By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.
We love him, because he first loved us.
Elder Bruce R. McConkie of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles wrote this in his book Mormon Doctrine, page 121. It is a book, not a conference talk.

Above all the attributes of godliness and perfection, charity is the one most devoutly to be desired. Charity is more than love, far more; it is everlasting love, perfect love, the pure love of Christ which endureth forever. It is love so centered in righteousness that the possessor has no aim or desire except for the eternal welfare of his own soul and for the souls of those around him.
When we receive His love, we have more to give.

story.title: Jesus blesses the little children

blocks.text: Parents brought their children to Jesus. The disciples thought He was too busy and tried to send them away.

And they brought young children to him, that he should touch them: and his disciples rebuked those that brought them. But when Jesus saw it, he was much displeased, and said unto them, Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God. Verily I say unto you, Whosoever shall not receive the kingdom of God as a little child, he shall not enter therein. And he took them up in his arms, put his hands upon them, and blessed them.
Jesus was never too busy for them. He picked them up and held them. That is how He sees each of us. We are never in the way.

story.title: The widow of Nain

blocks.text: A widow was walking in a funeral procession. Her only son had died. She had no husband and now no son.

And it came to pass the day after, that he went into a city called Nain; and many of his disciples went with him, and much people. Now when he came nigh to the gate of the city, behold, there was a dead man carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow: and much people of the city was with her. And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her, and said unto her, Weep not. And he came and touched the bier: and they that bare him stood still. And he said, Young man, I say unto thee, Arise. And he that was dead sat up, and began to speak. And he delivered him to his mother.
She did not ask Him for anything. He saw her, and He had compassion. His love noticed her need before she spoke. He notices ours too.

application.text: First, find a quiet moment today and tell Heavenly Father about something that hurts. Know that Jesus understands. Second, think of someone who may feel unseen. Notice them, as the Savior noticed the widow. Third, say their name in your prayers this week.

story.title: Jesus weeps with Mary

blocks.text: Lazarus had died. Mary came to Jesus, heartbroken. Jesus already knew He would raise Lazarus. But look at what He did first.

Then when Mary was come where Jesus was, and saw him, she fell down at his feet, saying unto him, Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died. When Jesus therefore saw her weeping, and the Jews also weeping which came with her, he groaned in the spirit, and was troubled, And said, Where have ye laid him? They said unto him, Lord, come and see. Jesus wept. Then said the Jews, Behold how he loved him!
He could have skipped the tears. He did not. He sat in their sorrow with them. That is what love does. It is willing to feel what someone else feels.

application.text: First, think of someone who is grieving or struggling. Take them a small gift, or sit with them. You do not need to say much. Second, when you are the one hurting, tell the Savior plainly. He already understands. Third, ask in prayer where you can give someone your “coat” this week.

opening.text: Imagine you are in deep water and cannot swim. Someone on the shore throws you a rope. You do not have to be strong. You only have to hold on, and they pull.
The love of Jesus Christ works like that rope. It reaches us where we are. I would like to talk about His love.

mainMessage.text: Jesus Christ loves each of us, and the Father sent Him because of that love. He gave His life to rescue us. He draws us in, He knows our troubles, and He does not let go of the rope. No matter how far we feel from Him, He is not far from us. And when we feel His love, we reach out for others.

blocks.text: The rope was thrown first.
We did not climb to God. He came down to us. John wrote that God gave His only Son so that we would not perish. And he wrote that the love began with God, not with us.
For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.

In this was manifested the love of God toward us, because that God sent his only begotten Son into the world, that we might live through him. Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.
Elder Neal A. Maxwell of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his talk “Lessons from Laman and Lemuel” from the October 1999 general conference.

The tree of life . . . is the love of God (see 1 Ne. 11:25). The love of God for His children is most profoundly expressed in His gift of Jesus as our Redeemer: ‘God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son’ (John 3:16). To partake of the love of God is to partake of Jesus’ Atonement and the emancipations and joys which it can bring.
He gave the gift before we knew we needed it.
The rescuer gave everything.
A rescuer sometimes risks his own life. Jesus did more. He gave His. As the good shepherd, He said He would lay down His life for the sheep. And He taught that this is the greatest love there is.

I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep. . . . I am the good shepherd, and know my sheep, and am known of mine. As the Father knoweth me, even so know I the Father: and I lay down my life for the sheep.
Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
Elder David B. Haight of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles asked this in his article “Remembering the Savior’s Atonement” in the April 1988 Ensign. It is a magazine article, not a conference talk.
How are we doing as members of the Church in remembering our Lord and Savior, His sacrifice, and our indebtedness to Him?
We remember Him each week at the sacrament. It is one way we say thank you.
He pulls us in close.
A rescue ends with an embrace. Lehi felt encircled in the arms of the Lord’s love. Mormon wrote about being clasped in the arms of Jesus. It is a picture of being held, safe and close.
But behold, the Lord hath redeemed my soul from hell; I have beheld his glory, and I am encircled about eternally in the arms of his love.

For I know that such will sorrow for the calamity of the house of Israel; yea, they will sorrow for the destruction of this people; they will sorrow that this people had not repented that they might have been clasped in the arms of Jesus.
Elder Russell M. Nelson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his talk “The Atonement” from the October 1996 general conference.

Rich meaning is found in study of the word atonement in the Semitic languages of Old Testament times. In Hebrew, the basic word for atonement is kaphar, a verb that means ‘to cover’ or ‘to forgive.’ Closely related is the Aramaic and Arabic word kafat, meaning ‘a close embrace’—no doubt related to the Egyptian ritual embrace. References to that embrace are evident in the Book of Mormon. One states that ‘the Lord hath redeemed my soul . . . ; I have beheld his glory, and I am encircled about eternally in the arms of his love.’ \[2 Nephi 1:15.\] Another proffers the glorious hope of our being ‘clasped in the arms of Jesus.’ \[Mormon 5:11.\]
The word for atonement means embrace. That says a lot about Him.
He knows the water.

The best rescuers have been in the water themselves. Alma taught that Jesus took on our pains and weaknesses so He would know how to help us. And Isaiah recorded the Lord saying that He cannot forget us. He has our names on His hands.

And he shall go forth, suffering pains and afflictions and temptations of every kind; and this that the word might be fulfilled which saith he will take upon him the pains and the sicknesses of his people. And he will take upon him death, that he may loose the bands of death which bind his people; and he will take upon him their infirmities, that his bowels may be filled with mercy, according to the flesh, that he may know according to the flesh how to succor his people according to their infirmities.

Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee. Behold, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands; thy walls are continually before me.
Elder Richard G. Scott of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his talk “To Be Healed” from the April 1994 general conference.

Faith in Christ means we trust Him; we trust His teachings. That leads to hope, and hope brings charity, the pure love of Christ—that peaceful feeling that comes when we sense His concern, His love, and His capacity to cure us or to ease our burdens with His healing power.
Trust Him. Hold on.
He does not let go.
Paul said he was sure of it. Nothing in life or death, nothing above or below, can separate us from the love of God in Christ. And the Lord said His arm is stretched out all the day long.

For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

Wo be unto the Gentiles, saith the Lord God of Hosts! For notwithstanding I shall lengthen out mine arm unto them from day to day, they will deny me; nevertheless, I will be merciful unto them, saith the Lord God, if they will repent and come unto me; for mine arm is lengthened out all the day long, saith the Lord God of Hosts.
Elder Jeffrey R. Holland of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his talk “Prophets in the Land Again” from the October 2006 general conference.

To all of you who think you are lost or without hope, or who think you have done too much that was too wrong for too long, to every one of you who worry that you are stranded somewhere on the wintry plains of life and have wrecked your handcart in the process, this conference calls out Jehovah’s unrelenting refrain, ‘\[My\] hand is stretched out still’ \[see Isaiah 5:25; 9:17, 21\]. ‘I shall lengthen out mine arm unto them,’ He said, ‘\[and even if they\] deny me; nevertheless, I will be merciful unto them, . . . if they will repent and come unto me; for mine arm is lengthened out all the day long, saith the Lord God of Hosts’ \[2 Nephi 28:32\]. His mercy endureth forever, and His hand is stretched out still. His is the pure love of Christ, the charity that never faileth, that compassion which endures even when all other strength disappears \[see Moroni 7:46–47\].
His hand is stretched out still. The rope is still there.
We throw the rope to others.
Once we have been pulled to shore, we look back and see others in the water. Jesus asked us to love as He loves. John said we love because He first loved us.
A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another. By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.
We love him, because he first loved us.
Elder Bruce R. McConkie of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles wrote this in his book Mormon Doctrine, page 121. It is a book, not a conference talk.

Above all the attributes of godliness and perfection, charity is the one most devoutly to be desired. Charity is more than love, far more; it is everlasting love, perfect love, the pure love of Christ which endureth forever. It is love so centered in righteousness that the possessor has no aim or desire except for the eternal welfare of his own soul and for the souls of those around him.
To love like Him is to want what is best for another, for good.

story.title: “Father, forgive them”

blocks.text: Jesus was nailed to a cross. Those around Him mocked Him and gambled for His clothes. What He said next is hard to imagine.

And when they were come to the place, which is called Calvary, there they crucified him, and the malefactors, one on the right hand, and the other on the left. Then said Jesus, Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do. And they parted his raiment, and cast lots.
In His worst hour, He prayed for the very people who hurt Him. If His love reached them, it can reach us. And it can help us forgive those who hurt us.

application.text: First, think of one person you find hard to love. Pray for them by name, even for a minute. Second, ask Heavenly Father to show you where you can “throw a rope” to someone this week. Third, hold on to your own rope. When you feel far away, say a short prayer and trust that He is close.

story.title: Jesus blesses the Nephite children

blocks.text: The Savior had come to the Nephites. After He taught and healed them, He turned His attention to the children.

And when he had said these words, he wept, and the multitude bare record of it, and he took their little children, one by one, and blessed them, and prayed unto the Father for them. And when he had done this he wept again; And he spake unto the multitude, and said unto them: Behold your little ones. And as they looked to behold they cast their eyes towards heaven, and they saw the heavens open, and they saw angels descending out of heaven as it were in the midst of fire; and they came down and encircled those little ones about, and they were encircled about with fire; and the angels did minister unto them.
He took them one by one. Not as a crowd. One by one. That is how He loves each of us. He knows each person, and He gives each one His full attention.

application.text: First, set a “place” for someone this week. Invite a neighbor, a new member, or someone who is alone. Second, remember that the Savior sees you one by one. Pray and tell Him what is on your heart. Third, write down one way you have felt His love, and share it with someone close.
